one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the state of two simultaneous peace processes. On the MILF front, the Bangsamoro Basic Law has received congressional approval, with the Senate and House versions still disparate; the bicameral conference committee will harmonize them for ratification when Congress resumes on July 23 -- the same day as the SONA. He urges the final version to satisfy the MILF's longing while avoiding the constitutional pitfalls that led the Supreme Court to debunk the MOA-AD in North Cotabato v. Government (October 14, 2008). On the NDFP front, the CPP was founded by Jose Maria Sison on December 26, 1968 in Alaminos, Pangasinan, espousing Marxist-Maoist ideology; its armed wing, the NPA, has sustained the 'longest-running communist insurgency in the world.' Peace negotiations opened with President Cory Aquino on December 10, 1986, continued under Ramos, formally opened in Brussels on June 26, 1995, and produced The Hague Declaration listing four agenda items: (1) human rights and international humanitarian law, (2) socioeconomic reforms, (3) political and constitutional reforms, and (4) end of hostilities. Of these, only the first has been completed -- CARHRIHL, signed March 16, 1998. He clarifies CARHRIHL's legal status: it is not a treaty (no Senate concurrence; Vienna Convention applies only to states) nor a final binding agreement, but an important milestone. The GRP can indirectly enforce it by invoking the Constitution's Articles II, III, and XIII and the ICESCR as generally accepted principles of international law forming part of the law of the land. Formal talks on the second topic -- socioeconomic reforms -- are scheduled to resume June 28, and the column previews the continuation.
